calculators.title: Centor score

bands.text: 0 or 1: low risk; no test needed
2 or 3: intermediate risk; rapid strep test

calculators.note: The adult threshold differs: Acute Pharyngitis tests adults at 3 or more, and NICE prescribes by score without a routine test (Centor 3 or 4: most likely to benefit from an antibiotic). Clinical decision rules are not reliable in children. At 3 to 14 and at 45 or older the scores differ; McIsaac's age adjustment decides.

calculators.title: McIsaac score (modified Centor)

bands.text: 1 or less: low risk; no test needed
2 or more: intermediate or high risk; rapid strep test

calculators.note: The Centor criteria plus a point at 3 to 14 and minus a point at 45 or older (Acute Pharyngitis). Streptococcal Pharyngitis's table lists no exudate item and subtracts the point only over 45. Testing may be omitted under 3 unless a sibling has confirmed strep.

calculators.title: Westley croup score

bands.text: 2 or less: mild, unless the stridor is at rest

sources.where: Evaluation, Tables 1 and 2 ("6-11 | Severe"; Table 2 prints ">12" for impending respiratory failure); Treatment / Management
Definitions of severity: severe croup at a Westley Croup Score of 6 to 11; impending respiratory failure "corresponding to a Westley Croup Score greater than 11"

calculators.note: This pathway treats stridor at rest as moderate to severe at any total, and a child goes home only with no stridor at rest.

nodes.ask: Throat, airway, facial swelling or nosebleed complaint in the ED. First move?
options: Airway first: look for drooling, stridor, distress or swelling; keep the patient calm
Examine the throat with a tongue depressor first, then decide how worried to be
Lie the patient flat on the trolley so that the mouth, neck and nose can be examined fully
Throat swab for a rapid strep test while the patient waits to be seen by a doctor
nodes.chainStep: Airway first: drooling, stridor, a tripod posture, a muffled voice, trismus or swelling; keep the patient calm, and let a patient in respiratory distress sit up; then vitals and circulation
nodes.why: Life-threatening causes come first: an abscess or epiglottitis shows itself with a muffled voice, drooling, stridor, a tripod posture, trismus or a stiff neck. Agitation is avoided in a child with stridor, and in suspected epiglottitis nobody lays the patient flat or examines or manipulates the pharynx before the airway is secured. In anaphylaxis most patients lie supine, but respiratory distress calls for sitting up. For a nosebleed the primary survey starts the same way: airway, then the circulation.

outcomes.if: Threatened airway; drooling, a tripod posture, stridor without a barking cough, or swelling under the jaw
Croup picture; barking cough and a hoarse voice in a young child, with or without stridor
Lip, tongue or face swelling; no stridor or drooling, with or without hives or wheeze
Choking; a sudden cough, gag or silence while eating or playing
Nosebleed; blood from the nose, with or without blood in the throat
Sore throat, airway safe; no drooling, stridor or distress

nodes.ask: Drooling, stridor or swelling under the jaw. First move?
options: Upright and calm; most skilled airway team now; plan for failure; no throat exam in a child
Lie them flat and look at the throat with a tongue depressor to see how swollen it really is
Send them to radiology for a lateral neck film before the airway team is called
Rapid sequence intubation in the ED now, before anesthesia or ENT arrives
nodes.chainStep: Upright and undisturbed, gentle oxygen, the most skilled airway clinicians (anesthesia and ENT) called, a plan for failure including front-of-neck access; no throat exam, IV line or film in a child with suspected epiglottitis
nodes.why: Examining the throat, lying flat, an IV line, imaging or agitation can turn a narrowed airway into a blocked one, so a child with suspected epiglottitis is left upright with gentle oxygen and no tongue blade. Intubating without the expertise of anesthesia and ENT backup is a recognized error. Imaging waits for the airway: in a child with suspected epiglottitis no lateral neck film is taken before the airway is controlled, and in Ludwig angina imaging has no part in the first assessment. Plan for failure from the start: in a cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate crisis, scalpel front-of-neck access follows without delay.

nodes.ask: Child with sudden fever, drooling and a tripod posture. Airway plan?
options: Controlled intubation in the operating room by anesthesia and ENT, tracheostomy ready
Lateral neck x-ray in radiology first, to look for a thumb sign before calling the team
Nebulized racemic epinephrine and dexamethasone in the ED, then reassess the stridor
IV line and blood cultures in the ED first, then intubation once the results return
nodes.chainStep: Controlled intubation in the operating room by anesthesia and ENT with a tracheostomy ready; blood and epiglottic cultures once the tube is in; ICU
nodes.why: Pediatric epiglottitis is a clinical diagnosis: no exam, laryngoscopy, lab test or film comes before the airway, and about 20% of lateral neck films miss it. The airway is ideally secured in the operating room, with a tracheostomy if intubation fails. Cultures and a blood count wait for a secured tube, and racemic epinephrine is among the things to avoid.

nodes.ask: Adult, severe pain on swallowing and a muffled voice; the mouth looks near normal. Next?
options: Flexible nasolaryngoscopy by ENT with the patient sitting up and anesthesia on hand
Rapid strep test, and oral penicillin V for 10 days if the result comes back positive
A normal-looking oropharynx excludes it; treat as a viral sore throat with analgesia
Nebulized racemic epinephrine, then reassess the voice and swallowing in an hour
nodes.chainStep: Close monitoring and flexible nasolaryngoscopy by ENT, sitting up, with an anesthesiologist available; a lateral neck film, if taken, fits epiglottitis at 7 mm or more
nodes.why: An adult who is not in extremis is monitored closely and examined with a flexible nasolaryngoscope by ENT, an anesthesiologist available; this has largely replaced the lateral neck film, which fits epiglottitis at a thickness of 7 mm. Adults often have fever without obvious signs in the mouth and can decompensate suddenly, even after antibiotics for a sore throat. Racemic epinephrine and agitation are avoided.

options: IV ceftriaxone or another third-generation cephalosporin
Oral penicillin V for 10 days, as for a strep throat
IV metronidazole alone, to cover the mouth anaerobes
IV dexamethasone alone, with antibiotics if the cultures grow
nodes.chainStep: IV ceftriaxone (or cefotaxime or cefuroxime) once the airway is stable, covering H influenzae, still the commonest cause in adults and children, vaccinated or not; ICU; adjust to cultures
nodes.why: Antibiotics follow airway stabilization: ceftriaxone or an equivalent, with cefuroxime, ceftriaxone or cefotaxime named for children. H influenzae is still the single most common cause in adults and children, and vaccinated children can still get it. Every patient goes to intensive care, intubated or not, with a tracheostomy tray at hand. Corticosteroids may reduce edema and shorten the intensive care stay.

nodes.summary: Epiglottitis: airway first (the operating room in a child; nasolaryngoscopy and ICU observation in most adults, with a surgical airway plan), then IV ceftriaxone or another third-generation cephalosporin, cultures and ICU care.

nodes.ask: Tense swelling under the jaw, raised floor of mouth, trismus, drooling. Airway?
options: Awake flexible fiberoptic nasotracheal intubation, surgical airway ready
Blind nasotracheal intubation to get past the swollen mouth quickly
A supraglottic airway device first, then a CT scan of the neck
IV antibiotics first, with intubation if stridor or cyanosis develops later
nodes.chainStep: Awake flexible fiberoptic nasotracheal intubation by an experienced clinician, cricothyrotomy or tracheostomy prepared first; then contrast CT, IV ampicillin-sulbactam or clindamycin, and drainage of any abscess
nodes.why: Asphyxiation is the leading cause of death in Ludwig angina, so the airway comes first. Awake flexible fiberoptic nasotracheal intubation is preferred, with a surgical airway prepared before any attempt. Blind nasal intubation can provoke bleeding, rupture an abscess and trigger laryngospasm, and a supraglottic device may not seat past the trismus. Stridor and cyanosis are late, ominous signs, not the trigger to act.

orders.item: Antibiotics, once the airway is secure
orders.dose: IV ampicillin-sulbactam or clindamycin; immunocompromised: cefepime, meropenem or piperacillin-tazobactam; add vancomycin or linezolid with MRSA risk
10 mg IV is the usual agent when used; not yet a standard of care
When imaging shows an abscess, there is fluctuance, or antibiotics alone fail

nodes.ask: Deep neck infection suspected; the airway is safe or secured. Imaging?
options: CT neck with IV contrast, an airway clinician alongside if at risk
CT neck without IV contrast, to spare the kidneys the dye load
Bedside needle aspiration of the back of the throat to find pus
Plain lateral neck film alone; a normal film settles the question for now
nodes.chainStep: CT neck with IV contrast (the gold standard), with a clinician trained in emergency airway management present if the airway is at risk; blood cultures; chest x-ray if chest pain or septic emboli are suspected
nodes.why: Contrast-enhanced CT is the gold standard for the source and extent of a deep neck infection; without contrast it separates cellulitis from abscess much less well. If the airway may be compromised, a clinician trained in emergency airway management stays with the patient in the scanner. In young children a lateral neck film or ultrasound often comes first, but the plain film misses about 1 in 5 (sensitivity 80%). The posterior pharynx is examined cautiously by airway-experienced clinicians, because an abscess can rupture and be aspirated.

orders.dose: Aerobic and anaerobic when a retropharyngeal abscess is suspected; with any sign of sepsis
Chest pain (mediastinal spread) or suspected septic emboli

outcomes.if: Abscess; a rim-enhancing collection

orders.dose: Airway compromise: immediate incision and drainage. Otherwise all but the smallest abscesses usually need drainage, above all if not better after 24 to 48 hours of IV antibiotics or larger than 2 to 2.5 cm

outcomes.if: Phlegmon; cellulitis, no drainable collection

orders.dose: IV antibiotics; drain if no improvement after 48 hours or a collection forms

outcomes.if: Internal jugular thrombosis; septic thrombophlebitis in the neck

orders.dose: A beta-lactamase-resistant beta-lactam; clindamycin or metronidazole with a significant beta-lactam allergy. Lemierre chapter: about 6 weeks for most; Deep Neck Infections: 3 to 6 weeks
Not for uncomplicated disease; usually for cerebral sinus extension, large or bilateral clot, or no improvement in 72 hours

outcomes.if: No deep neck infection; no collection, phlegmon or clot

nodes.summary: Deep neck infection: airway first, then admission, IV ampicillin-sulbactam or clindamycin (MRSA cover when at risk) and ENT; drain a discrete abscess, at once if the airway is compromised, while a phlegmon often settles on antibiotics alone. In Ludwig angina, decompress when imaging shows an abscess or antibiotics fail.

Lemierre syndrome: blood cultures, a chest film for septic emboli, and IV antibiotics that resist beta-lactamase for 3 to 6 weeks; drain any abscess; anticoagulate only for extensive or spreading clot or no improvement by 72 hours.
No collection, phlegmon or clot on contrast CT: a deep neck infection is unlikely; look for another cause of the pain and fever.

outcomes.if: Peritonsillar abscess; one tonsil pushed in, uvula deviated, trismus, hot potato voice
Neck swelling after a sore throat; fever, rigors, tender swelling at the jaw angle
Mono picture; teen or young adult, fatigue, cervical nodes, enlarged spleen
Pharyngitis; none of the abscess, neck or mono signs

nodes.ask: One tonsil pushed in, uvula deviated, trismus; airway safe or secured. Next?
options: Needle aspiration or incision and drainage, plus antibiotics
Rapid strep test, with antibiotics if the result comes back positive
Drain it, with no antibiotic needed once the pus is out
IV dexamethasone alone, with antibiotics if the fever persists
nodes.chainStep: Drainage by needle aspiration or incision and drainage (upright, topical anesthetic), plus antibiotics such as clindamycin, ampicillin-sulbactam or amoxicillin-clavulanate; analgesia, IV fluids; consider a steroid
nodes.why: With drooling, tripoding or labored breathing, the airway is stabilized before anything else. Once the abscess is diagnosed, clinically or on imaging, prompt antibiotics are essential, alongside drainage and supportive care. Needle aspiration and incision and drainage are both used; incision may bring fewer recurrences. Ultrasound can confirm the abscess and guide the needle, and contrast CT is for an unclear picture or a suspected deeper infection. Corticosteroids reduce pain and shorten recovery alongside the antibiotic, which remains essential.

orders.dose: Dexamethasone 8 to 10 mg IV three times daily or methylprednisolone 2 to 3 mg/kg IV; eases pain and shortens recovery
Point-of-care ultrasound first; contrast CT if ultrasound is nondiagnostic, the picture is unclear or another deep space infection is suspected

Acute Pharyngitis and Stridor in Children: drainage is necessary. Peritonsillar Abscess: the choice is individualized; no significant outcome difference between medical and surgical management, and abscesses over 2 cm resolve less often on medicine alone
orders.note: The StatPearls chapters disagree on whether every peritonsillar abscess needs drainage.

nodes.summary: Peritonsillar abscess: needle aspiration or incision and drainage, antibiotics covering strep and the mouth anaerobes, analgesia and fluids; airway first if there is distress.

nodes.ask: Exudative sore throat, fatigue, cervical nodes and an enlarged spleen. Next?
options: EBV testing (heterophile or EBV-specific antibody); no amoxicillin
Amoxicillin for 10 days in case this is strep, then review in the clinic
A routine oral corticosteroid course to shorten the illness
Oral acyclovir to clear the virus and shorten the illness
nodes.chainStep: EBV testing (EBV-specific antibodies, or a heterophile test), HIV testing; supportive care with acetaminophen or an NSAID; no amoxicillin; no contact sports until cleared
nodes.why: Laboratory confirmation is advised for everyone with suspected mononucleosis, because the diagnosis shapes counseling on the course and the risk of splenic rupture. EBV-specific antibodies are the more accurate test; the heterophile (Monospot) test is cheaper and faster but less sensitive, and often negative in young children. Treatment is supportive: antivirals have no established role, routine corticosteroids are not recommended, antibiotics are not indicated, and amoxicillin brings a maculopapular rash in up to 30%.

orders.dose: For everyone with a mononucleosis picture; HIV RNA if EBV and HIV antibody/antigen tests are negative
Confirm with EBV-specific antibodies; test for group A strep and HIV
Not indicated; a maculopapular rash in up to 30%
Mononucleosis chapter: back after 4 weeks from symptom onset, strenuous activity after 3 weeks. EBV chapter: a minimum of 3 weeks and full resolution of splenomegaly
orders.note: The two StatPearls chapters give 4 weeks and 3 weeks.

orders.dose: Emergency airway management and surgical consultation; high-dose corticosteroid may help

nodes.summary: Infectious mononucleosis: EBV testing and an HIV test, supportive care with acetaminophen or an NSAID, no antibiotics (amoxicillin brings a rash), and no contact sports for at least 3 to 4 weeks because of the rare splenic rupture.

nodes.ask: Sore throat with no abscess, neck or mono signs. Who needs a strep test?
options: Score it (McIsaac, or Centor at 15 to 44); test if 2 or more
Antistreptolysin O titers to confirm a recent streptococcal infection
Start penicillin on tonsillar exudate alone, without a test
A cough or a runny nose rules strep out; no score is needed
nodes.chainStep: McIsaac score (the Centor criteria with the age adjustment, equal to Centor at 15 to 44): 1 or less, no test and no antibiotic; 2 or more, a rapid strep test
nodes.why: History and examination alone cannot diagnose group A strep, and cough, runny nose or hoarseness make it less likely without ruling it out. A Centor or McIsaac score sorts risk: 0 or 1 is low and needs no test; intermediate (2 to 3) or high (4) risk gets a rapid antigen test. Antistreptococcal antibody titers reflect past infection and are not recommended.

orders.dose: 1 point each: tonsillar exudates, tender anterior cervical nodes, fever (temperature over 38 C, 100.4 F), absence of cough
Centor plus 1 point for age 3 to 14, minus 1 point for age 45 or older

Streptococcal Pharyngitis: test at a Centor or McIsaac of 2 or more. Acute Pharyngitis: test adults at a Centor of 3 or more. NICE NG84: rapid tests not recommended for routine use; Centor 0 to 2, no antibiotic; Centor 3 or 4, consider an immediate or back-up antibiotic
orders.note: The sources disagree on the adult testing threshold, and NICE prescribes by score without testing. Acute Pharyngitis adds that scores cannot replace testing in children and adolescents.

orders.dose: Testing may be omitted (low risk of strep and rheumatic fever), unless a sibling has confirmed strep

outcomes.if: Low risk; McIsaac 1 or less (equal to Centor at 15 to 44)
Intermediate or high risk; McIsaac 2 or more (equal to Centor at 15 to 44)

nodes.ask: McIsaac 2 or more. Next?
options: Rapid strep test; a throat culture if negative in a child
CT of the neck with IV contrast first, to look for a deep abscess
Heterophile (Monospot) test in place of a strep test
Blood count and CRP to sort bacterial from viral
nodes.chainStep: Swab both tonsils and the posterior pharynx for a rapid antigen test or NAAT before any antibiotic; a backup throat culture in a child with a negative rapid antigen test
nodes.why: The rapid antigen test is the primary diagnostic test whichever score is used, and it is highly specific; a NAAT is an alternative. The swab takes both tonsils and the posterior pharynx before any antibiotic. Adults and older adolescents have less strep and an extremely low risk of rheumatic fever, so a negative result needs no culture, while a child with a negative rapid test gets a confirmatory culture. Imaging is kept for instability, trouble swallowing or a stiff neck.

orders.dose: Acute Pharyngitis: a confirmatory throat culture is necessary in a child with a negative rapid test; adults and older adolescents do not need one. Streptococcal Pharyngitis: a culture may be performed in a child with a negative rapid test (AAP Red Book 2025), though earlier papers found it not cost-effective for preventing rheumatic fever
orders.note: Acute Pharyngitis calls the backup culture necessary; Streptococcal Pharyngitis says it may be performed.

outcomes.if: Positive; group A strep
Negative; a child also gets a backup culture

nodes.ask: Group A strep confirmed; no penicillin allergy. Antibiotic?
options: Penicillin V or amoxicillin, by mouth for 10 days
Azithromycin by mouth, once a day for 5 days
Amoxicillin-clavulanate by mouth, twice a day for 10 days
Clindamycin by mouth, three times a day for 10 days
nodes.chainStep: Penicillin V or amoxicillin for 10 days, or a single IM dose of benzathine penicillin G; acetaminophen or an NSAID; back to school or work after 24 hours of antibiotic
nodes.why: Penicillin or amoxicillin is first line: penicillin is the only antibiotic shown to cut rheumatic fever, and no penicillin resistance has been documented. A 10-day course clears the throat better than 5 to 7 days. Broad-spectrum antibiotics do not reduce treatment failure, and macrolides and clindamycin are for penicillin allergy, with resistance widely documented.

orders.dose: NICE NG84 by age: 1 to 11 months 62.5 mg four times a day or 125 mg twice a day; 1 to 5 years 125 mg four times a day or 250 mg twice a day; 6 to 11 years 250 mg four times a day or 500 mg twice a day; 12 to 17 years 500 mg four times a day or 1,000 mg twice a day; 5 to 10 days. Streptococcal Pharyngitis: 250 mg 2 to 3 times a day for 10 days. Acute Pharyngitis: 27 kg or less 250 mg 2 to 3 times a day, over 27 kg 500 mg 2 to 3 times a day, for 10 days
orders.note: Three sources print three child regimens: by age band (NICE), one dose for all children (Streptococcal Pharyngitis), and by weight (Acute Pharyngitis).

orders.dose: Streptococcal Pharyngitis: 250 mg 4 times daily or 500 mg twice daily for 10 days. Acute Pharyngitis: 500 mg 2 to 3 times a day for 10 days. NICE (adults): 500 mg four times a day or 1,000 mg twice a day for 5 to 10 days
orders.note: Three sources print three adult doses; NICE adds that 5 days may be enough for symptoms but 10 days may clear the throat better.

orders.dose: Acute Pharyngitis: 50 mg/kg/day (maximum 1,000 mg/day) once daily or in 2 divided doses, for 10 days. Streptococcal Pharyngitis: 50 mg/kg/day (maximum 1,000 mg/day) for 10 days, or 50 mg/kg (maximum 500 mg) twice daily
orders.note: Both chapters give 50 mg/kg/day once daily; Acute Pharyngitis splits that total into 2 doses, while the Streptococcal Pharyngitis twice-daily line gives 50 mg/kg a dose, double the daily total.

orders.dose: 500 mg twice a day for 10 days
One IM dose: 600,000 units under 27 kg; 1.2 million units over 27 kg and in adults (the chapters differ at exactly 27 kg)
orders.note: At exactly 27 kg the chapters differ: Acute Pharyngitis gives 600,000 units at 27 kg or less; Streptococcal Pharyngitis gives 1.2 million units at 27 kg or more.

orders.dose: Cephalexin 20 mg/kg twice daily (maximum 500 mg a dose) or cefadroxil 30 mg/kg once daily (maximum 1 g a day), for 10 days
No cephalexin or cefadroxil; clindamycin (child 7 mg/kg a dose 3 times a day, maximum 300 mg a dose; adult 300 mg 3 times a day) for 10 days, or a macrolide

Streptococcal Pharyngitis: 12 mg/kg on day 1 (maximum 500 mg), then 6 mg/kg (maximum 250 mg) on days 2 to 5. Acute Pharyngitis: 12 mg/kg a day (maximum 500 mg) for 3 days; adults 500 mg a day for 3 days. NICE prefers clarithromycin 250 to 500 mg twice a day for 5 days (adults)
orders.note: The two StatPearls chapters print different azithromycin courses (5 days and 3 days).

orders.dose: Acetaminophen or an NSAID; no routine corticosteroid

nodes.summary: Strep pharyngitis: penicillin V or amoxicillin for 10 days (cephalexin for a mild allergy; a macrolide or clindamycin after an immediate reaction), analgesia, back to school or work after 24 hours of treatment; reassess if not better within 5 days.

Low score or a negative test: no antibiotic; acetaminophen or an NSAID and fluids, with the usual course of about a week; seek help if it worsens or has not started to improve after a week. A child with a negative rapid test is treated only if the backup culture grows group A strep.

outcomes.if: Mild; no stridor at rest, Westley 2 or less
Moderate to severe; stridor at rest, or Westley 3 or more

orders.dose: Intubation with a tube 0.5 size smaller than usual for age and size

nodes.ask: Croup, no stridor at rest (Westley 2 or less). Treatment?
options: Oral dexamethasone as a single dose, then home
Nebulized albuterol (salbutamol), repeated until the stridor settles
Nebulized epinephrine, then home right after the dose
A cough syrup with dextromethorphan at bedtime
nodes.chainStep: Oral dexamethasone once (0.6 mg/kg is the usual dose; 0.15 and 0.3 mg/kg appear as effective); supportive care; home
nodes.why: Mild croup gets a single dose of dexamethasone and supportive care, by mouth unless the child cannot swallow, is vomiting or is in severe distress. Doses of 0.15, 0.3 and 0.6 mg/kg appear equally effective, 0.6 mg/kg being the usual one. Nebulized epinephrine is not necessary for mild croup, beta-agonists can worsen upper airway obstruction, and cough medicines are discouraged.

sources.where: Treatment / Management, Steroids; Cough Medicine; Pearls and Other Issues

orders.dose: One dose by mouth; 0.6 mg/kg most common; 0.15, 0.3 and 0.6 mg/kg appear equally effective; maximum not stated in this pathway's sources

nodes.ask: Croup with stridor at rest or a Westley score of 3 or more. Treatment?
options: Nebulized epinephrine plus dexamethasone, then observe
Nebulized albuterol plus dexamethasone, then observe
Heliox first, holding epinephrine and steroids for later
Intubation now, with a tube a half size smaller
nodes.chainStep: Nebulized epinephrine (racemic, or L-epinephrine 1:1000) plus dexamethasone; blow-by oxygen if the saturation is low; observe 3 to 4 hours after the last epinephrine; admit if not improving
nodes.why: Moderate to severe croup gets nebulized epinephrine as well as dexamethasone, and stridor at rest is a warning sign: going home needs no stridor at rest. Epinephrine improves symptoms within 30 minutes, but the effect may fade after 2 hours, so the child is observed for 3 to 4 hours after the last dose before going home. Beta-agonists can worsen the obstruction, heliox is a bridge only when distress persists despite treatment, and intubation is rare (about 0.2%).

sources.where: Treatment / Management; Pearls and Other Issues

Blind finger sweeps can push the object down toward the larynx.

nodes.chainStep: Airway first; two large-bore IV lines with crystalloid; blood count, type and crossmatch, coagulation studies; reverse anticoagulation when clinically appropriate; nasal packing (posterior if needed); ENT; admit
nodes.why: Airway first, then the circulation: moderate to severe bleeding gets 2 large-bore lines and crystalloid, with a blood count, crossmatch and clotting studies that never delay treatment. In a life-threatening bleed the priority is stopping it with packing, posterior if needed, and transfusion may be needed. Lying flat with the head back sends blood into the throat, where it is swallowed or aspirated. Imaging has no role in the emergency control of active epistaxis, and cauterizing both sides of the septum risks a perforation.

nodes.chainStep: Sit up, lean forward, pinch the soft (cartilaginous) nose for 10 to 15 minutes; suction clots; a topical vasoconstrictor such as oxymetazoline if it keeps bleeding; on an anticoagulant, check the INR
nodes.why: Most anterior nosebleeds stop with pressure. The patient leans forward, so blood is not swallowed or aspirated, and pinches the cartilaginous nose, not the bony bridge, for 10 to 15 minutes. If that fails, clots are suctioned and a topical vasoconstrictor such as oxymetazoline goes on, with more pressure. Packing is for bleeding that pressure, vasoconstrictors or cautery have not stopped, and silver nitrate goes on one side of the septum only.

nodes.why: Packing is indicated when pressure, vasoconstrictors or cautery fail, or no source can be seen. Resorbable materials suit patients on antithrombotic drugs or with a coagulopathy, since they spare the mucosa and need no removal. A pack that turns bright red, blood past it, or swallowing blood after 30 to 60 minutes means it has failed. Posterior packing, embolization and surgery are for bleeding anterior packing cannot control, and imaging has no role in the emergency.
